title: Trigonometry I: The Sine Rule
summary: How to label any triangle and use the sine rule to find a missing side or angle, including the ambiguous case.

p: In triangle ABC, the angles are written with capital letters A, B, C at the corners. The sides are written with small letters. Side a is opposite angle A, side b is opposite angle B and side c is opposite angle C.
The sine and cosine rules work for every triangle, not only for right-angled ones. Remember that the angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.

img.alt: A triangle with corners A, B and C and the sides a, b and c opposite them
img.cap: Side a is opposite angle A, and so on.

p: In any triangle, a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C. You can also turn it upside down: sin A / a = sin B / b = sin C / c. Use the upside-down form when you are finding an angle.
Use the sine rule when you know (1) two angles and one side, or (2) two sides and an angle opposite one of them.
In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 8 cm. Find b. a / sin A = b / sin B, so b = 8 × sin 65° / sin 40° = 8 × 0.9063 / 0.6428 = 11.28 cm.

In triangle XYZ, X = 35°, Y = 75° and z = 20 cm. Find Z, x and y. Z = 180° − 35° − 75° = 70°. x = 20 × sin 35° / sin 70° = 20 × 0.5736 / 0.9397 = 12.21 cm. y = 20 × sin 75° / sin 70° = 20 × 0.9659 / 0.9397 = 20.56 cm. (The largest side, 20.56, is opposite the largest angle, 75°.)

sections.h: Example 3: finding an angle and the ambiguous case
p: In triangle ABC, a = 10 cm, b = 14 cm and A = 38°. Find B. sin B / b = sin A / a, so sin B = 14 × sin 38° / 10 = 14 × 0.6157 / 10 = 0.8619. Your calculator gives B = 59.5°. But sin of an angle is also positive in the second quadrant, so B = 180° − 59.5° = 120.5° is also possible. Is it? 38° + 120.5° = 158.5°, which is less than 180°, so the triangle can exist.

Both answers are correct: there are two possible triangles. This is called the ambiguous case. (Some books say that B must be acute because b is larger than a. That is not correct: b > a only tells us that B is larger than A.) When the question does not give a diagram or other information, give both answers.

title: The Cosine Rule
summary: Using the cosine rule to find a side when two sides and the angle between them are known, or to find an angle when all three sides are known.

p: In any triangle ABC: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, b² = a² + c² − 2ac cos B and c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
To find an angle, rearrange it: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc).
Use the cosine rule when you know (1) two sides and the angle between them (SAS) to find the third side, or (2) all three sides (SSS) to find an angle.
If the angle is 90°, then cos 90° = 0 and the rule becomes Pythagoras: a² = b² + c².
Two sides of a triangle are 8 cm and 11 cm and the angle between them is 64°. The third side: a² = 64 + 121 − 2 × 8 × 11 × cos 64° = 185 − 176 × 0.4384 = 185 − 77.15 = 107.85. a = 10.39 cm.

A triangle has sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. The largest angle is opposite the longest side. cos B = (5² + 7² − 9²) / (2 × 5 × 7) = (25 + 49 − 81) / 70 = −7 / 70 = −0.1. The negative answer tells us that the angle is obtuse: B = 95.74°.
Be careful with the calculator: work out the product 2bc cos A first, then subtract it. Writing (b² + c² − 2bc) first and then multiplying by cos A is a common mistake.

summary: How to decide between the sine and cosine rules, how to find the area of a triangle using two sides and the included angle, and problems on land and distances.

p: Use the table to choose. Always draw and label the triangle first.

p: 1. Draw and label the triangle. 2. List what is given and what is wanted. 3. Choose the rule. 4. Substitute carefully. 5. Calculate and check that the answer is sensible: the longest side must be opposite the largest angle.
Area = ½ × a × b × sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b. The same applies to the other two pairs of sides.
Example. Two sides of 8 cm and 11 cm with 64° between them. Area = ½ × 8 × 11 × sin 64° = 44 × 0.8988 = 39.55 cm².

Check with the 13, 14, 15 triangle. The angle opposite 13 is 53.13°, between the sides 14 and 15. Area = ½ × 14 × 15 × sin 53.13° = 105 × 0.8 = 84 cm². This is the well-known area of the 13, 14, 15 triangle.

Sides 13, 14, 15. The largest angle is opposite 15: cos = (13² + 14² − 15²) / (2 × 13 × 14) = 140 / 364 = 0.3846, so the angle is 67.38°. The smallest angle is opposite 13: 53.13°. The third angle is 180° − 67.38° − 53.13° = 59.49°.

A plot of land is a triangle. Two sides measure 18 m and 24 m and the angle between them is 58°. Third side² = 18² + 24² − 2 × 18 × 24 × cos 58° = 324 + 576 − 864 × 0.5299 = 900 − 457.85 = 442.15. The third side is 21.03 m. The area is ½ × 18 × 24 × sin 58° = 216 × 0.8480 = 183.2 m².

title: Trigonometry II: Pythagoras and the Trigonometric Ratios
summary: A review of Pythagoras' theorem and of sine, cosine and tangent in right-angled triangles, with values for 30°, 45° and 60°.

p: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides: c² = a² + b².

Example 1. Legs 3 and 4: c² = 9 + 16 = 25, c = 5. Example 2. Hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5: other leg² = 169 − 25 = 144, so the other leg = 12. These are Pythagorean triples: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17).
Name the sides from the point of view of the angle θ: the hypotenuse is the longest side, the opposite is the side facing θ, and the adjacent is the side next to θ (not the hypotenuse).
sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse. cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse. tan θ = opposite / adjacent. A way to remember: SOH CAH TOA.

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with the angle theta marked and the sides labelled adjacent, opposite and hypotenuse, with the formulas sin, cos and tan

p: These values come from the equilateral triangle and the square and are worth learning.
sin θ = cos (90° − θ). For example sin 30° = cos 60° = 0.5.
A right-angled triangle has an angle of 35° and the adjacent side is 7 cm. Opposite = 7 × tan 35° = 7 × 0.7002 = 4.90 cm. Hypotenuse = 7 / cos 35° = 7 / 0.8192 = 8.55 cm.

Opposite 5 and adjacent 12: tan θ = 5/12 = 0.4167, so θ = 22.62°. If cos θ = 0.6 then θ = 53.13°. With hypotenuse 10 cm and an angle of 30°: opposite = 10 × sin 30° = 5 cm and adjacent = 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 cm.

title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
summary: Using trigonometry to find heights and distances when we look up at an object (elevation) or look down at it (depression).

p: The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look UP at an object. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look DOWN at an object.

Both angles are measured from the horizontal line, never from the vertical. The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point P on the ground is equal to the angle of depression of P from the top of the tower, because they are alternate angles between parallel lines (the ground and the horizontal from the top).

img.alt: An observer on the ground looking up at the top of a tower, showing the angle of elevation at the observer and the equal angle of depression at the top of the tower
img.cap: Angle of elevation = angle of depression.

p: 1. Draw a clear diagram with a horizontal line and a vertical line. 2. Mark the angle and the lengths. 3. Find the right-angled triangle. 4. Choose sine, cosine or tangent. 5. Solve and give the answer with units.
From a point 50 m from the foot of a flagpole, the angle of elevation of its top is 35°. Height = 50 × tan 35° = 50 × 0.7002 = 35.0 m.
A ladder 6 m long makes an angle of 65° with the ground. Height reached = 6 × sin 65° = 5.44 m. Distance of its foot from the wall = 6 × cos 65° = 2.54 m.
From the top of a cliff 40 m high, the angle of depression of a boat is 25°. The boat is a distance d from the foot of the cliff. tan 25° = 40 / d, so d = 40 / tan 25° = 40 / 0.4663 = 85.78 m.

From a point A the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30°. From a point B, 20 m nearer to the tower (in the same straight line), it is 45°. Let the tower be h m high and let B be d m from its foot. From B: h = d (since tan 45° = 1). From A: h = (d + 20) tan 30° = 0.5774 (d + 20). So d = 0.5774 d + 11.547, which gives 0.4226 d = 11.547 and d = 27.32 m. The tower is 27.3 m high.

title: Algebraic Fractions: Simplifying, Adding and Subtracting
summary: Simplifying fractions by factorising, and adding and subtracting algebraic fractions with a common denominator.

p: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. We find a common denominator (the LCM of 2 and 3 is 6), write each fraction with it, and add the tops. Algebraic fractions work in the same way.
To simplify, factorise the top and the bottom completely, then cancel common factors. You can only cancel factors that multiply the whole top and the whole bottom, never terms that are added.
Wrong: (x + 3)/3 does not simplify to x + 1. The 3 in the top is added, not multiplied.
Example 1. 1/x + 2/(x + 1). The common denominator is x(x + 1). 1/x = (x + 1) / (x(x + 1)) and 2/(x + 1) = 2x / (x(x + 1)). Sum = (x + 1 + 2x) / (x(x + 1)) = (3x + 1) / (x(x + 1)).
Example 2. x/3 + (x + 1)/4. The common denominator is 12. = 4x/12 + 3(x + 1)/12 = (4x + 3x + 3)/12 = (7x + 3)/12.

Example. 3/(x − 1) − 2/(x + 2). The common denominator is (x − 1)(x + 2). = (3(x + 2) − 2(x − 1)) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)) = (3x + 6 − 2x + 2) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)) = (x + 8) / ((x − 1)(x + 2)). Take care with the minus sign: it changes the sign of every term in the second bracket.
A denominator can never be 0. In (x − 3)/(x − 2), x cannot be 2.

title: Multiplying and Dividing Algebraic Fractions
summary: Multiply tops and bottoms after factorising and cancelling; to divide, turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.

p: Factorise everything first, cancel, then multiply the tops together and the bottoms together.
Example 1. (x + 2)/(x − 1) × (x − 1)/(x + 3). The (x − 1) cancels. Answer: (x + 2)/(x + 3).
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal (turn it upside down). A ÷ (B/C) = A × C/B.
Do not turn over the first fraction. Do not cancel across a plus or minus sign. Do not forget to factorise before cancelling.

title: Equations with Fractions and Everyday Problems
summary: Solving equations that contain fractions by multiplying by the common denominator, and using fractions to solve work, money and tank problems.

p: Find the lowest common denominator of all fractions. Multiply every term on both sides by it to remove the fractions. Solve the resulting equation. Check your answer in the original equation (and that it does not make a denominator zero).
x/2 + x/3 = 10. Multiply by 6: 3x + 2x = 60, so 5x = 60 and x = 12. Check: 6 + 4 = 10. Correct.
(x + 1)/3 = (x − 1)/2. Cross-multiply: 2(x + 1) = 3(x − 1), so 2x + 2 = 3x − 3 and x = 5. Check: 6/3 = 2 and 4/2 = 2. Correct.
2/(x − 1) = 3/(x + 2). Cross-multiply: 2(x + 2) = 3(x − 1), so 2x + 4 = 3x − 3 and x = 7. Check: 2/6 = 1/3 and 3/9 = 1/3. Correct.
1/2 + 1/x = 3/4. Multiply every term by 4x: 2x + 4 = 3x, so x = 4. Check: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. Correct.
Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 3 hours. Together they fill 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 of the tank each hour. So the tank is full in 2 hours.
Ade can do a job in 10 days and Bola can do it in 15 days. In one day they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the job. Together they take 6 days.

A man spends 1/3 of his salary on rent and 1/4 on food. He has ₦25 000 left. Fraction left = 1 − 1/3 − 1/4 = 12/12 − 4/12 − 3/12 = 5/12. So 5/12 of the salary is ₦25 000 and the salary is 25 000 × 12 / 5 = ₦60 000. Check: rent ₦20 000, food ₦15 000, left ₦25 000. Total ₦60 000.

title: Further Trigonometry: Bearings
summary: What a bearing is, how to write bearings with three figures, how to change compass directions to bearings and how to find a back bearing.

p: A bearing is a direction. It is measured as an angle clockwise from North. A bearing is written with three figures, so 65° is written 065° and 5° is written 005°. Due North is 000°.
To find the bearing of B from A: stand at A, face North, and turn clockwise until you face B. The angle you turn through is the bearing. Draw a North line at A, not at B.

img.alt: A North arrow from point O with the angle 065 degrees to point A and 290 degrees to point B, both measured clockwise from North
img.cap: Bearings are measured clockwise from North.

p: Eight main directions have these bearings.
Sometimes a direction is written from North or South towards East or West, for example N30°E. Start at N (or S) and turn the given angle towards E (or W).
The back bearing is the bearing of the starting point seen from the finishing point. Because the two North lines are parallel, the back bearing differs by 180°.
If the bearing is less than 180°, add 180°. If it is 180° or more, subtract 180°.
Example 1. The bearing of B from A is 070°. The bearing of A from B is 070° + 180° = 250°.
Example 2. If the bearing is 125°, the back bearing is 305°. If it is 310°, the back bearing is 130°.

title: Navigation Problems
summary: Using bearings with Pythagoras, trigonometry and the sine and cosine rules to find distances between ships, planes and towns.

p: 1. Draw a North line at each place where the direction changes. 2. Mark the bearings and distances. 3. Find the angle inside the triangle by using the rules about parallel lines and angles on a straight line. 4. Use Pythagoras, trigonometry, or the sine or cosine rule. Distance = speed × time.

A ship sails 20 km North and then 15 km East. The distance from the start is √(20² + 15²) = √625 = 25 km. The bearing of the final point from the start: tan θ = 15/20 = 0.75, so θ = 36.87°. The bearing is 037° (to the nearest degree).

Two ships leave a port at the same time. One travels at 30 km/h on a bearing of 040° and the other at 25 km/h on a bearing of 130°. How far apart are they after 2 hours? First ship: 30 × 2 = 60 km. Second ship: 25 × 2 = 50 km. The angle between their paths is 130° − 40° = 90°, so by Pythagoras, d² = 60² + 50² = 3 600 + 2 500 = 6 100 and d = 78.10 km.

A boat sails 40 km on a bearing of 065° and then 30 km on a bearing of 140°. How far is it from its starting point? The angle inside the triangle at the turning point is 180° − (140° − 65°) = 180° − 75° = 105°. By the cosine rule, d² = 40² + 30² − 2 × 40 × 30 × cos 105° = 1 600 + 900 + 2 400 × 0.2588 = 2 500 + 621.2 = 3 121.2. d = 55.87 km.

sections.h: Example 4: finding a bearing back home
p: A plane flies 40 km on a bearing of 060° and then 30 km on a bearing of 150°. The turn is 90°, so the distance from start is √(40² + 30²) = 50 km. The angle at the start between the first leg and the line to the end is tan⁻¹(30/40) = 36.87°. The bearing of the end point from the start is 060° + 36.87° = 096.87°, about 097°. The bearing of the start from the end (the way home) is 097° + 180° = 277°.

title: Chords, Arcs, Distance and Direction
summary: Using trigonometry to find the length of a chord or an arc, and to split a journey into east and north parts.

p: A chord AB subtends an angle θ at the centre O of a circle of radius r. Draw OM perpendicular to AB. M is the midpoint, and the angle AOM is θ/2. So AM = r sin (θ/2), and chord AB = 2r sin (θ/2).
Example 1. r = 8 cm and θ = 60°. Chord = 2 × 8 × sin 30° = 8 cm. (The triangle OAB is equilateral, so the chord equals the radius.)
Example 2. r = 10 cm and θ = 80°. Chord = 2 × 10 × sin 40° = 20 × 0.6428 = 12.86 cm.
Example 3. r = 13 cm and the chord is 24 cm. sin (θ/2) = 12/13 = 0.9231, so θ/2 = 67.38° and θ = 134.76°, about 134.8°.

Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr. Example. r = 10 cm and θ = 80°. Arc = (80/360) × 2 × 3.1416 × 10 = 0.2222 × 62.83 = 13.96 cm. Notice that the arc (13.96 cm) is a little longer than the chord (12.86 cm), as it should be.

sections.h: Distance and direction: east and north parts
p: A journey on a bearing can be split into two parts. For a distance d on a bearing θ: the East part = d sin θ and the North part = d cos θ. (For bearings above 90° these may be negative: a negative North part means going South.)

Example. A town B is 30 km from A on a bearing of 050°. East part = 30 × sin 50° = 30 × 0.7660 = 22.98 km. North part = 30 × cos 50° = 30 × 0.6428 = 19.28 km. B is about 23.0 km east and 19.3 km north of A.
Reverse example. A man walks 5 km east and 12 km north. The distance is √(25 + 144) = 13 km. tan θ = 5/12, so θ = 22.62°. The bearing is 023°.
